item.title: CVE-2026-48282 Exploitation, Cavern Manticore, and DragonReturn Lead Cyber Threats
item.content:encoded:
Max severity Adobe ColdFusion flaw now exploited in attacks — Must Read

Attackers are now exploiting CVE-2026-48282, a maximum-severity Adobe ColdFusion flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution on unpatched systems. Adobe and Canada’s Cyber Centre urge administrators to apply the latest ColdFusion updates immediately.

  • Attackers are exploiting the maximum-severity Adobe ColdFusion vulnerability CVE-2026-48282, according to a warning from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.
  • CVE-2026-48282 affects Adobe ColdFusion versions 2025.9, 2023.20, and earlier, and can allow attackers without privileges to gain remote code execution on unpatched systems.
  • Adobe released security updates for the vulnerability and recommended that administrators install them as soon as possible, such as within 72 hours.
  • The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-48282 is being exploited and encouraged users and administrators to apply the necessary updates.
  • Shadowserver tracks nearly 800 Adobe ColdFusion instances exposed online, but the article says it is not known how many are honeypots or have been secured against CVE-2026-48282 attacks.

Cavern Manticore: Exposing Iran-Linked Modular C2 Framework — Must Read

Check Point Research details Cavern Manticore, an Iran-linked threat actor targeting Israeli government and IT organizations with a modular .NET C2 framework that abuses RMM tools and DLL sideloading for initial access. The framework’s unusual mix of .NET Framework, C++/CLI, and NativeAOT modules enables stealthy post-exploitation capabilities such as file, database, LDAP, network reconnaissance, credential testing, and tunneling while complicating analysis and detection.

  • Check Point Research tracks Cavern Manticore as an Iran-nexus threat actor targeting Israeli organizations, especially in the government and IT sectors.
  • Cavern Manticore used a modular .NET command-and-control framework with components compiled as .NET Framework, Mixed-Mode C++/CLI, and .NET 8 NativeAOT binaries.
  • The observed execution chain abused SysAid’s software update feature to deploy a WinDirStat DLL sideloading package in which a trojanized uxtheme.dll acted as the Cavern Agent.
  • The framework’s modules provide post-exploitation capabilities including file system browsing, database enumeration and querying, LDAP and Active Directory reconnaissance, network reconnaissance, SMB credential brute-forcing, and SOCKS5/WebSocket tunneling.
  • The article reports that in multiple observed intrusions, the initial foothold was achieved through abuse of existing Remote Monitoring and Management software deployed in the targeted organization.

Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT — Must Read

A suspected China-linked campaign is targeting Indian taxpayers and finance professionals with fake Income Tax Department lures that install DcRAT through a malicious tax-filing utility. The operation uses DLL sideloading, anti-analysis checks, image-based payload concealment, persistence, and data exfiltration to steal sensitive information.

  • Seqrite Labs observed a suspected China-nexus campaign, codenamed Operation DragonReturn, targeting Indian taxpayers, tax professionals, and corporate finance teams starting on May 18, 2026.
  • The campaign uses spear-phishing emails impersonating the Income Tax Department of India and links to a fake tax-related site that delivers a ZIP archive posing as an official offline tax-filing utility.
  • The malicious archive uses DLL sideloading to run nvdaHelperRemote.dll, inject another payload into memory, retrieve a JPG file from 204.194.48[.]250, and extract a secondary DLL hidden inside the image.
  • The malware copies itself as Mixed Reality.exe, creates an auto-start Windows service named MixedSvc, and deploys payloads including a .NET loader that disables Windows AMSI scanning and loads DCRat.
  • Seqrite Labs said the campaign shows infrastructure and tactical overlaps with Silver Fox, while LevelBlue separately reported ValleyRAT campaigns using fake installers and salary-themed phishing emails against Chinese- and Japanese-speaking users.

Ukrainian media outlets now among 'priority targets' for Russian hackers — Should Read

Ukraine’s SBU warned that media outlets have become priority targets for Russian hackers, citing recent DDoS and phishing attempts against major TV broadcasters. Ukrainian media are also facing continued physical damage from Russian missile and drone strikes.

  • Ukraine's SBU said media organizations have become one of the priority targets for Russian hackers.
  • Volodymyr Karastelyov, head of the SBU's cyber department, disclosed two previously unreported cyberattacks targeting Ukrainian television broadcasters, including a DDoS attack on a nationwide channel and a phishing campaign against a leading television group.
  • The SBU said it has neutralized more than 16,000 cyberattacks and cyber incidents targeting Ukrainian government agencies, financial institutions, defense organizations, and media outlets since Russia's full-scale invasion.
  • Ukraine's SSSCIP reported last year that Russian hackers had carried out more than 200 successful cyberattacks against Ukrainian media organizations since the start of the invasion.
  • The National Union of Journalists of Ukraine documented 80 incidents in the first half of this year in which Russian attacks damaged media infrastructure or affected journalists carrying out their work.

A Phishing Link Wearing Two Security Vendors' Badges: Inside a Benefits-Enrollment Credential Lure — Should Read

A phishing email impersonating Regions Bank used clean Amazon SES authentication and hid its credential-harvesting destination behind nested Egress Defend and Barracuda link-protection wrappers. The key takeaway is that trusted security-vendor rewrite domains can launder malicious links, so defenses must decode redirect chains and assess message context rather than relying on visible URL reputation or SPF/DKIM/DMARC alone.

  • A phishing email used Regions Bank branding to present a same-day benefits-enrollment deadline to a finance team at a hospitality organization.
  • The email authenticated successfully through Amazon SES using the unrelated Saudi-registered domain hatmi.sa, with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passing.
  • The Complete Enrollment button pointed first to an Egress Defend rewrite URL, which contained a Barracuda Link Protection URL, which in turn contained an encoded target domain of aemf.org.
  • The article states that visible URL reputation checks can be bypassed when a malicious destination is hidden behind trusted security-vendor link wrappers.
  • The reporting user flagged the suspicious email, four mailboxes were quarantined, and the laundered link did not receive a click.

Use Case Deep Dive: Your EDR Fired on an IP. Here’s How to Know if it’s Part of Something Bigger. — Optional

When an EDR alert flags an IP address, analysts should enrich and correlate it with related infrastructure, indicators, and historical activity to determine whether it is an isolated event or part of a broader threat campaign.

  • The article is presented as a use case deep dive.
  • The article focuses on a situation where an EDR alert fires on an IP address.
  • The article discusses how to determine whether the flagged IP address is part of something larger.

How to Evaluate an AI SOC Platform in 2026: 6 Capabilities That Separate Leaders from Bolt-On AI solutions — Optional

The article argues that buyers evaluating AI SOC platforms should look past marketing claims and test whether agents can perform detection, triage, investigation, and response using real-time correlated security context with auditable outcomes. It promotes Exaforce as an example of this agentic SOC approach.

  • The article defines an AI SOC platform as a security operations platform where AI agents carry out detection, triage, investigation, and response by reasoning over correlated security data under human oversight.
  • The article says buyers should test whether a platform has a real-time, correlated data foundation that connects identity, configuration, resource, and behavioral baseline data before alerts occur.
  • The article recommends evaluating whether agents can handle the full incident lifecycle, preserve context across detection, triage, investigation, and response, and provide evidence-backed verdicts that analysts can audit.
  • The article argues that strong AI SOC platforms should cover data sources beyond the SIEM, support staged autonomy with human approval for sensitive actions, and produce measurable improvements such as lower false-positive rates and faster investigation and response times.
  • The article presents Exaforce as an example of an agentic AI SOC platform, describing its Exabots for detection, triage, investigation, and response and citing customer outcomes such as reduced investigation time and a 14-minute mean time to respond for P0 incidents.

Mid-Year Threat Trends: What H1 2026 Signals for the Rest of the Year — Optional

Cyble says H1 2026 showed ransomware, access brokers, identity-based attacks, geopolitically driven operations, and AI-enabled threats scaling faster and becoming more coordinated. Security teams should prepare for continued growth in identity abuse, rapid exploitation, and hybrid cyber activity through the rest of 2026.

  • In March 2026, Cyble recorded 702 ransomware attacks and 54 major data breaches and leaks worldwide, with Qilin, Akira, The Gentlemen, Dragonforce, and INC Ransom responsible for more than 56% of the ransomware activity.
  • In Q1 2026, the Americas saw 1,305 cyber incidents, including 1,138 publicly claimed ransomware attacks, and five groups drove 58% of that ransomware volume.
  • Cyble observed 20 incidents of access to compromised networks being sold on underground forums in March 2026, with professional services and retail as the most commonly listed sectors.
  • The article says attackers increasingly rely on credential theft, MFA bypass, session hijacking, and third-party access abuse, meaning they are often logging in instead of breaking in.
  • During the February 2026 Middle East escalation, internet connectivity in targeted regions dropped to 1–4% of normal levels, more than 70 hacktivist groups became involved, navigation disruption affected over 1,100 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, and more than 8,000 conflict-themed domains were registered.

Integrations of the Month — Optional

Silent Push is promoting new integrations with Splunk, Tines, and ServiceNow that bring its preemptive threat intelligence and IOFA data directly into detection, automation, and incident-response workflows. The main message is that these integrations help teams identify, enrich, route, and block adversary infrastructure before it is used in attacks.

  • Silent Push highlights three integrations with Splunk, Tines, and ServiceNow that are designed to place preemptive threat data inside tools security teams already use.
  • The Splunk integration feeds Indicators of Future Attack and Traffic Origin data into Splunk as enrichment data so detection rules can act on infrastructure being staged before it reaches an environment.
  • The Tines integration exposes Silent Push Context Graph data as Tines actions, enabling automated alert enrichment, case routing, low-risk closure, and proactive blocking workflows without writing code.
  • The ServiceNow integration attaches Context Graph data to tickets for suspicious domains or IPs, including a risk score, related adversary campaigns, threat actor associations, matching IOFA patterns, and connected infrastructure.
  • Silent Push says its Threat Check API shows an average of 154 days between when it identifies infrastructure and when that infrastructure appears in other feeds, with a median of 117 days.

6th July – Threat Intelligence Report — Optional

This weekly threat intelligence roundup highlights major ransomware and data breach incidents alongside emerging AI-enabled threats and actively exploited critical vulnerabilities in Oracle E-Business Suite, Citrix NetScaler, Linux, and Progress Kemp LoadMaster. Organizations should prioritize patching exposed systems and monitoring for ransomware, supply-chain malware, and credential-theft activity.

  • River Bank & Trust experienced a ransomware incident after an unauthorized actor accessed the network of parent company River Financial Corporation on June 16.
  • Aflac disclosed a data breach affecting its Japan operations after attackers accessed its policyholder portal between June 15 and June 25, exposing personal and financial data of nearly 4.4 million customers.
  • Check Point Research demonstrated a browser-native ransomware technique generated by a large language model that abuses Chrome’s File System Access API to read, exfiltrate, and encrypt photos inside the browser on Android and Windows.
  • Oracle E-Business Suite is affected by CVE-2026-46817, a critical remote code execution flaw reportedly exploited against about 950 internet-exposed instances worldwide.
  • Researchers described a North Korea-aligned supply-chain campaign called PolinRider that published 108 malicious packages and a Chrome extension across open-source registries.

Community Bootcamp: Live View - Inspect a suspicious URL right now — Optional

This appears to be an announcement for a community bootcamp session focused on using Live View to inspect a suspicious URL in real time.

  • The article is titled “Community Bootcamp: Live View - Inspect a suspicious URL right now.”
  • The title identifies the item as a Community Bootcamp session.
  • The title says the bootcamp focuses on using Live View.
  • The title says the session involves inspecting a suspicious URL.
